1a.html:
Why statistics. A ceramic breaks at its most severe flaw (weakest link). Flaws vary randomly in size, position and orientation, so nominally identical specimens fail at different stresses (slide 10). One strength value with a safety factor (deterministic design) therefore fails; strength must be given as a probability.

Weibull distribution (slide 11).

P_f = 1 - \exp\left[-\frac{V}{V_0}\left(\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_0}\right)^m\right]

\sigma_0 is the characteristic strength (P_f = 0.632 at V = V_0) and m the Weibull modulus.

What m measures. m is the slope of \ln\ln(1/P_s) against \ln\sigma, found by ranking at least 30 results with P_f = j/(N + 1). High m means a narrow strength band and a predictable, reliable material; low m means wide scatter. Ceramics have m \approx 5 to 20, steels about 100.

Use in design. The allowable stress for an accepted failure probability is

\sigma = \sigma_0\left[\ln\frac{1}{1 - P_f}\right]^{1/m}

For 1 failure in 1000 this is 0.25\sigma_0 at m = 5 but 0.71\sigma_0 at m = 20. Strength also falls with size, \sigma \propto V^{-1/m}: ten times the volume is 37 % weaker at m = 5, 11 % at m = 20. Hence bend strengths exceed tensile ones (slide 9).

Limits. One flaw population, test conditions matching service, and no slow crack growth are assumed; proof testing and stress-probability-time diagrams cover these.
pts: Strength is statistical: weakest-link failure from randomly distributed flaws gives scatter, so deterministic design fails
Weibull equation with \sigma_0 (P_f = 0.632) and m defined
m is the slope of \ln\ln(1/P_s) against \ln\sigma from ranked tests (about 30 or more)
High m = narrow distribution = reliable; ceramics 5 to 20 against about 100 for steels
Design use: \sigma = \sigma_0[\ln(1/(1 - P_f))]^{1/m}, with a comparison such as 0.25\sigma_0 at m = 5 against 0.71\sigma_0 at m = 20
Size effect \sigma \propto V^{-1/m} (larger for low m), or bend strength above tensile strength
Limitations: several flaw populations, service conditions, slow crack growth; proof testing or SPT diagrams
1a.src: Mechanical properties, slides 9-11; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 317-320
1a.watch:
• m describes scatter, not the strength level: a material can have a high mean strength and a low m.
  • Survival P_s = 1 - P_f goes inside the double logarithm.

1b.html:
No. In a truly brittle material (linear elastic to fracture, K_{IC} independent of crack length, a flat R-curve) a higher K_{IC} raises every strength by the same factor. The Weibull line moves to higher stress but keeps its slope m.

Justification

  1. Each specimen fails when its critical flaw reaches K_I = K_{IC} (slide 6):
\sigma_f = \frac{K_{IC}}{Y\sqrt{\pi c}}
  1. K_{IC} is a material constant, the same in every specimen, so the scatter in \sigma_f comes only from the scatter in flaw size c (and shape, Y) between specimens.
  2. If K_{IC} becomes kK_{IC} with the same flaws, every \sigma_f becomes k\sigma_f, and every point on the plot of \ln\ln(1/P_s) against \ln\sigma shifts by \ln k:
P_f = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{\sigma}{k\sigma_0}\right)^m\right]

Only \sigma_0 changes; m and the relative scatter stay the same.

  1. m is set by the flaw population. If the number of flaws per volume longer than c falls as c^{-q}, the critical size c^* \propto (K_{IC}/\sigma)^2 gives P_f depending on (\sigma/K_{IC})^{2q}: m = 2q, while K_{IC} enters only \sigma_0.

When m does rise. Toughening with a rising R-curve (transformation toughening, crack bridging) makes strength insensitive to the initial flaw size. Scatter then narrows and m rises, but such a material is no longer truly brittle. Narrowing the flaw distribution (cleaner processing, better finish) also raises m.
pts: Clear answer: no, m is unchanged for a truly brittle (flat R-curve) material
Uses \sigma_f = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c}): strength scatter comes only from the flaw-size distribution, since K_{IC} is a constant
Raising K_{IC} by k multiplies every strength by k: Weibull line shifts by \ln k, same slope; \sigma_0 becomes k\sigma_0
States that m is fixed by the flaw population (for example m = 2q for a c^{-q} flaw distribution), independent of K_{IC}
Exception: rising R-curve toughening (transformation, bridging) makes strength flaw-tolerant and raises m
Conclusion: higher K_{IC} raises the strength level (and survival at a fixed stress), not the scatter; m rises only if the flaw spread narrows
1b.src: Mechanical properties, slides 6, 10-11; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 317-319, 344-345
1b.watch:
• Do not confuse "stronger" with "more reliable in the Weibull sense": at a fixed service stress the tougher part does survive more often, because \sigma_0 rose, but its m is the same.
  • If the change that raised K_{IC} (a new grain size or second phase) also changed the flaws, m can change; that is a flaw effect, not a toughness effect.

1c.html:
Given: alumina bars 100 \times 10 \times 5\ \mathrm{mm} in uniform tension, mean strength \bar{\sigma}_1 = 320\ \mathrm{MPa}, Weibull modulus m = 16. New bars: 5 \times 5\ \mathrm{mm} section, 75\ \mathrm{mm} long, same material and test.

Find: the mean failure stress \bar{\sigma}_2 of the new bars (a) with flaws spread through the volume, (b) with all strength-limiting flaws on the surface.

Step 1, size effect. Failure starts at the worst flaw (weakest link, slide 10), so the survival probability depends on how much material is stressed:

P_s = \exp\left[-\frac{V}{V_0}\left(\frac{\sigma}{\sigma_0}\right)^m\right]

Equal survival probability in both sizes needs V_1\sigma_1^{\,m} = V_2\sigma_2^{\,m}:

\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} = \left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right)^{1/m}

The mean strength is \bar{\sigma} = \sigma_0 (V_0/V)^{1/m}\,\Gamma(1 + 1/m), so means scale the same way (the \Gamma factor cancels).

Step 2, volume flaws.

\begin{aligned} V_1 &= 100 \times 10 \times 5 = 5000\ \mathrm{mm^3}, \qquad V_2 = 75 \times 5 \times 5 = 1875\ \mathrm{mm^3} \\ \frac{V_1}{V_2} &= 2.667, \qquad (2.667)^{1/16} = \exp\left(\frac{0.9808}{16}\right) = 1.0632 \\ \bar{\sigma}_2 &= 320\ \mathrm{MPa} \times 1.0632 = 340\ \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}

Step 3, surface flaws. The flaws now sample the stressed surface area A, so \sigma_2/\sigma_1 = (A_1/A_2)^{1/m}:

\begin{aligned} A_1 &= 2(100 \times 10 + 100 \times 5 + 10 \times 5) = 3100\ \mathrm{mm^2} \\ A_2 &= 2(75 \times 5 + 75 \times 5 + 5 \times 5) = 1550\ \mathrm{mm^2} \\ \bar{\sigma}_2 &= 320\ \mathrm{MPa} \times 2^{1/16} = 320\ \mathrm{MPa} \times 1.0443 = 334\ \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 340 MPa if the flaws are in the volume, and about 334 MPa if they are all on the surface. The smaller bar is stronger because it is less likely to hold a large flaw. The gain is smaller for surface flaws because the area halves while the volume falls by 2.67.
pts: States the weakest-link size effect, P_s = \exp[-(V/V_0)(\sigma/\sigma_0)^m], so equal failure probability needs V\sigma^m constant
Derives \sigma_2/\sigma_1 = (V_1/V_2)^{1/m} and notes that it also holds for the mean strength
Correct volumes, 5000 and 1875\ \mathrm{mm^3} (ratio 2.67)
Volume-flaw answer: factor 1.063, \bar{\sigma}_2 \approx 340\ \mathrm{MPa}
For surface flaws uses the stressed area, \sigma_2/\sigma_1 = (A_1/A_2)^{1/m}
Correct areas, 3100 and 1550\ \mathrm{mm^2} (ratio 2.0)
Surface-flaw answer: factor 1.044, \bar{\sigma}_2 \approx 334\ \mathrm{MPa}, with the reason the smaller bar is stronger
1c.src: Mechanical properties, slides 9-11; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 317-319
1c.watch:
• The exponent is 1/m, not m: (2.67)^{16} would give an absurd strength.
  • Whether the gripped ends count does not matter here: the side faces alone give 3000 and 1500\ \mathrm{mm^2}, again a ratio of 2.
  • The scaling assumes the same flaw population in both sets (same powder, firing and surface finish). A different machining finish on the small bars changes \sigma_0 and possibly m.

2a.fix: Slide 13 gives the monoclinic cell volume as about 139.3\ \text{\AA}^3. Its own lattice parameters give abc\sin\beta = 5.15 \times 5.21 \times 5.31 \times \sin 99.2^\circ = 140.6\ \text{\AA}^3, so the t \rightarrow m expansion from the tetragonal 134.2\ \text{\AA}^3 (the same four-formula cell, 2a^2c) is about 4.8 %, not the 3.8 % the printed volume implies. The usual figure for this transformation is about 4 to 5 %.
2a.html:
What toughening needs. Zirconia is toughened only by the stress-induced t \rightarrow m transformation of metastable tetragonal grains or precipitates at a crack tip (slides 13-15). The change is martensitic, with about 4 to 5 % volume expansion and a shear strain of about 0.16. Constrained by the matrix, it squeezes the crack tip and wake (shielding):

\Delta K_T = A\,V_t\,\varepsilon^{T} E\sqrt{w}

Pure and fully stabilised zirconia contain no metastable t (V_t = 0), so \Delta K_T = 0.

Pure \mathrm{ZrO_2}. It is monoclinic (m) below about 1170^\circ\mathrm{C}, tetragonal (t) up to 2370^\circ\mathrm{C} and cubic (c) above. Sintered in the t field, the whole body turns to m on its own during cooling (near 950^\circ\mathrm{C}), and the uncontrolled expansion cracks it. At room temperature it is already stable m, so a crack meets nothing that can transform: low strength and low K_{IC}.

Fully stabilised zirconia (FSZ). About 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} or more (or about 15 mol% CaO) makes the cubic fluorite phase stable from the firing temperature to room temperature. Cubic is the equilibrium phase and has no transformation to trigger, so the crack runs through brittle cubic grains: K_{IC} \approx 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}, like ordinary oxides.

Contrast. Partial stabilisation (3 to 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3}, slide 15) keeps fine metastable t in a cubic matrix, and K_{IC} rises to 6 to 15\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}.
pts: Toughening needs metastable t that transforms to m under the crack-tip stress, its expansion compressing the crack (shielding)
Pure \mathrm{ZrO_2} polymorphs: m below about 1170^\circ\mathrm{C}, t, and c above about 2370^\circ\mathrm{C}
Pure zirconia transforms t to m spontaneously on cooling, and the expansion (4 to 5 %; 3 to 5 % accepted) cracks the part
At room temperature pure zirconia is all stable m, so nothing is left to transform at a crack tip
FSZ (about 8 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3} or more) is cubic down to room temperature; cubic has no stress-induced transformation, K_{IC} \approx 3\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}
Contrasts with PSZ or TZP, which retain metastable t (K_{IC} 6 to 15\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}), or shows this on the phase diagram
2a.src: Mechanical properties, slides 12-15; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 344, 351-352
2a.watch:
• The printed question reads "Why do you zirconia"; it means pure zirconia, as in the 2018-19 paper.
  • Do not say yttria toughens zirconia: it only stabilises t or c (slide 15). Too much yttria gives FSZ, too little gives pure-zirconia behaviour.
  • Pure \mathrm{ZrO_2} can stay tetragonal in powders finer than a few tens of nanometres (surface energy), but not in sintered parts.

3a.html:
Hydrothermal synthesis crystallises an oxide powder directly from water (a solution, gel or suspension of precursors) heated above 100^\circ\mathrm{C} in a sealed vessel. Heat and pressure raise solubility and reactivity, so the crystalline product precipitates without calcination.

Conditions

  1. Autoclave: thick-walled steel with an inert liner (PTFE up to about 250^\circ\mathrm{C}; Ag, Au or Pt above) against corrosion and contamination.
  2. Temperature: 100 to 374^\circ\mathrm{C} (critical point of water), typically 150 to 350^\circ\mathrm{C}; higher temperature raises solubility, rate and crystallinity.
  3. Pressure: autogenous, the saturated vapour pressure (1.6 MPa at 200^\circ\mathrm{C}, 8.6 MPa at 300^\circ\mathrm{C}, 22 MPa at the critical point), limited by the degree of fill (about 50 to 85%).
  4. Solution chemistry: precursors (salts, hydroxides, gels, fine oxides), concentration, pH and a mineraliser (NaOH, KOH, \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}, KF) to dissolve the oxide. \mathrm{BaTiO_3} forms from \mathrm{TiO_2} in \mathrm{Ba(OH)_2} only in strongly alkaline, \mathrm{CO_2}-free solution.
  5. Supersaturation control: heating rate, holding time (hours), stirring and seeds set nucleation against growth, hence size and shape.
  6. Recovery: cool, filter, wash and dry.

Result: fine (tens of nm to 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}), crystalline, narrowly sized, weakly agglomerated powders, for example \mathrm{BaTiO_3} and 3 mol% \mathrm{Y_2O_3}-\mathrm{ZrO_2} (Carter Fig 20.14).
pts: Defines the process: crystallisation from aqueous solution or suspension above 100^\circ\mathrm{C} under pressure in a sealed vessel
Autoclave with an inert liner (PTFE, Ag, Pt) against corrosion and contamination
Temperature 100 to 374^\circ\mathrm{C} (typically 150 to 350), with the reason (solubility, rate, crystallinity)
Autogenous pressure equal to the saturated vapour pressure (MPa range), set by the degree of fill
Solution chemistry: precursors, concentration, pH and a mineraliser
Supersaturation control by time, heating rate, stirring and seeds to set particle size and shape
Product: crystalline, fine, narrow-sized, weakly agglomerated powder without calcination, with an example
3a.src: Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 382, 530-532; Standard textbook treatment
3a.watch:
• The slides do not cover hydrothermal synthesis; Carter describes the same equipment for growing quartz crystals (0.5 M NaOH, about 400^\circ\mathrm{C}, 80% fill, a 40^\circ\mathrm{C} gradient), and the powder route uses the same vessel, usually isothermal, cooler (150 to 350^\circ\mathrm{C}) and without seeds.
  • Above 374^\circ\mathrm{C} and 22.1 MPa water is supercritical; that variant gives even finer particles because solubility drops sharply.
  • The Bayer process (digesting bauxite in NaOH at about 150 to 250^\circ\mathrm{C}) is an industrial hydrothermal process.

3b.html:
In vapour-phase synthesis, gaseous reactants (for example \mathrm{TiCl_4} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{TiO_2} + 2\mathrm{Cl_2}, or 3\mathrm{SiH_4} + 4\mathrm{NH_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{Si_3N_4} + 12\mathrm{H_2}) react, nucleate and grow into particles. The heat source sets the reaction temperature, the heating and cooling rates and the residence time, and so particle size, size distribution, agglomeration, purity and cost.

Heat sourceProsCons
Furnace (hot-wall tube reactor)simple, cheap, uniform and easily controlled temperature; continuousslow heating and long residence time give coarser, aggregated, broadly sized particles; reaction and deposits on hot walls contaminate; limited to about 1500^\circ\mathrm{C}
Flame (combustion, flame hydrolysis of chlorides)cheapest per kg, very high throughput (fumed \mathrm{SiO_2}, \mathrm{TiO_2} pigment), 1500 to 2500^\circ\mathrm{C}oxidising, water-rich gas: oxides only; strong temperature gradients give a wider size range and hard, necked aggregates; Cl or C residues
Thermal plasma (DC arc or RF induction)very high temperature (several thousand to 10{,}000 K) evaporates refractory precursors; inert or reactive gas gives nitrides and carbides; fast quench gives ultrafine (below 20 nm) particles; RF has no electrodes, so it is cleanhigh power cost; steep gradients give broad size distributions and agglomerates; DC electrode erosion contaminates; hard to control and scale
Laser (\mathrm{CO_2} laser pyrolysis)small, sharply defined reaction zone away from walls, so high purity; very fast heating and cooling (about 10^6 K/s) and uniform short residence time give fine, spherical, narrowly sized, unagglomerated powders, oxides and nonoxidesreactant must absorb the 10.6 \mum beam (\mathrm{SiH_4} does); costly, low production rate

Choice: flame for bulk oxides, plasma for refractory and nonoxide nanopowders, laser for the highest-quality small batches, furnace for simple laboratory synthesis. All vapour routes are costlier than chemical solution routes but give high-purity, discrete nanoparticles (Carter).
pts: States that the heat source controls temperature, heating and cooling rate and residence time, hence size, distribution, agglomeration, purity and cost
Furnace: simple and controllable, but slow heating, wall reactions, aggregation and limited temperature
Flame: cheap and high-throughput (fumed silica, \mathrm{TiO_2}), but oxides only, wide size range and hard aggregates
Plasma: very high temperature, nonoxides and refractory materials, fast quench to nanoparticles, RF electrode-free; but costly, broad distribution, electrode contamination for DC
Laser: well-defined wall-free reaction zone, rapid heating, narrow size distribution and high purity; but needs an absorbing reactant, costly and slow
Concludes which source suits which product
3b.src: Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 372, 378-379; Standard textbook treatment
3b.watch:
• The slides do not cover this; the answer follows the standard classification of gas-phase reactors (furnace, flame, plasma, laser). Carter also shows evaporation-condensation (gas-condensation) chambers, where the heat source only evaporates the material; mention them if time allows.
  • Do not confuse a plasma reactor for powders with plasma-enhanced CVD of films; the heat source question is about making particles.

4a.html:
Ideal against real strength. Breaking bonds across a perfect plane needs the theoretical strength \sigma_{th} = \sqrt{E\gamma/a_0} \approx E/10: about 38 GPa for \mathrm{Al_2O_3}. Polycrystalline alumina breaks near 0.4 GPa, and most ceramics at E/100 to E/1000. Flaws make the difference.

1. Stress concentration (slide 7). At the tip of a crack of length c and tip radius \rho (Inglis):

\sigma_{max} \approx 2\sigma\sqrt{c/\rho}

Ceramic cracks stay atomically sharp because no dislocation plasticity blunts them (slide 4); for c = 50\ \mu\mathrm{m} and \rho \approx 0.2\ \mathrm{nm} (one atomic spacing) the factor is about 1000. The tip reaches \sigma_{th} while the applied stress is low.

2. Griffith and K_{IC} (slides 6-7). The crack runs when the released elastic energy pays for the new surfaces:

\sigma_f = \sqrt{\frac{2E\gamma}{\pi c}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma_f = \frac{K_{IC}}{Y\sqrt{\pi c}}

Strength falls as c^{-1/2}: with K_{IC} = 4\ \mathrm{MPa\,m^{1/2}}, an internal crack with c = 10\ \mu\mathrm{m} allows 714 MPa, c = 100\ \mu\mathrm{m} only 226 MPa.

3. Internal against surface flaws. Internal flaws (pores, inclusions, agglomerates, large grains, firing cracks) come from processing. Surface flaws (grinding damage, scratches, handling, corrosion) are usually worse: Y \approx 1.12, so a surface crack of depth c acts like an internal crack 2.5c long. In bending the highest tension is also at the surface (slide 8).

4. Tension against compression. Tension opens cracks normal to it, and growth is unstable; compression closes them, and failure needs many cracks to grow stably and link. Compressive strength is about ten times the tensile.

5. Porosity and grain size (slides 2-3). Pores remove load-bearing area and concentrate stress, so strength falls faster than density (\sigma \approx \sigma_0 e^{-bP}, b \approx 4 to 7). Large grains carry larger flaws, \sigma \propto d^{-1/2}.

6. Statistics and time. The worst flaw in the stressed volume controls failure, giving scatter (Weibull) and a size effect: \sigma_{\text{3-point}} > \sigma_{\text{4-point}} > \sigma_{\text{tension}} (slides 9-11). In moist air the flaws grow slowly under load (static fatigue).

K_{IC} is a material property (slide 6); flaws cut strength, not the intrinsic toughness. Finer powders, dense fine grains, careful finishing, compressive surfaces and proof testing raise strength.
pts: Theoretical strength \sigma_{th} \approx \sqrt{E\gamma/a_0} \approx E/10 against measured E/100 to E/1000 (for example 38 against 0.4 GPa for alumina)
Inglis stress concentration \sigma_{max} \approx 2\sigma\sqrt{c/\rho}; sharp cracks with no plastic blunting, factor about 1000
Griffith or fracture mechanics: \sigma_f = \sqrt{2E\gamma/\pi c} = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c}), strength \propto c^{-1/2}, with a number
Internal flaws (pores, inclusions, large grains) against surface flaws (machining, handling, Y \approx 1.12, worse; highest bending tension at the surface)
Tension opens cracks (unstable mode I growth); compression closes them, so compressive strength is much higher
Porosity (lost area and stress concentration, strength falls faster than density) and grain size (\sigma \propto d^{-1/2})
Worst flaw controls failure: scatter, Weibull statistics and the size effect
Time-dependent loss by subcritical crack growth (static fatigue)
States that flaws lower strength, not the intrinsic K_{IC}, or lists remedies (processing, finishing, compressive surface, proof testing)
4a.src: Mechanical properties, slides 2-11; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 305-306, 341-346
4a.watch:
• The question says flaws reduce strength "and fracture toughness". K_{IC} is a property of the material; flaws set the strength through \sigma_f = K_{IC}/(Y\sqrt{\pi c}) (slide 6, strength is not toughness).
  • c is the depth of a surface crack but the half-length of an internal one; say which you use.

4b.html:
Ceramics are elastic up to fracture at room temperature (slide 1): plastic flow is difficult because dislocations are hard to make and move, and complex because the response depends on many variables and mechanisms.

Difficult

  1. Strong ionic or covalent bonds give narrow dislocations and a high Peierls-Nabarro stress: about 10^{-2}\mu in \mathrm{Al_2O_3} and SiC against 10^{-4}\mu in metals.
  2. Charge: slip must avoid putting like ions face to face, so only some systems work (MgO and NaCl at room temperature: {110}\langle 1\bar{1}0\rangle, not {100}\langle 100\rangle).
  3. Large Burgers vectors (0.48 nm in \mathrm{Al_2O_3}) make dislocations costly (\propto \mu b^2), few and easily pinned.
  4. Von Mises: a polycrystal needs five independent slip systems; MgO and \mathrm{Al_2O_3} have two at room temperature, so slip blocked at grain boundaries opens cracks. Flaws reach K_{IC} first.

Complex

  • Behaviour changes with temperature and rate (slip in \mathrm{Al_2O_3} only above about 1200^\circ\mathrm{C}; polycrystalline MgO brittle to about 1700^\circ\mathrm{C}), structure, impurities and grain size.
  • Other mechanisms take over: twinning, transformation (\mathrm{ZrO_2}), diffusional creep, grain-boundary sliding and viscous flow of glass.
pts: Ceramics are elastic to fracture at room temperature; plastic flow needs mobile dislocations, which are scarce
Strong bonds: high Peierls-Nabarro stress (about 10^{-2}\mu against 10^{-4}\mu in metals)
Like-ion repulsion limits slip systems (MgO {110}\langle 1\bar{1}0\rangle), with a sketch
Large Burgers vector, high dislocation energy
Fewer than five independent slip systems (von Mises), so polycrystals crack at grain boundaries
Complex: depends on temperature, rate, structure, impurities and grain size, and other mechanisms (creep, twinning, transformation, viscous flow) take over
4b.src: Mechanical properties, slides 1, 4; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 232, 324-330, 337
4b.watch:
• The quotation is not on the slides; the points come from the course text, so confidence is medium on what the examiner stresses.
  • Do not say ceramics have no dislocations: single crystals of MgO and LiF bend at room temperature.

4c.html:
The curves. The bond energy is U(r) = -A/r^n + B/r^m with m > n (attraction plus short-range repulsion). The force between the atoms is

F = \frac{dU}{dr}

taken positive for net attraction, which an applied tension must balance. F = 0 at the equilibrium spacing r_0, the bottom of the energy well.

Stiffness: the slope at r_0. For small stretches F \approx S_0(r - r_0), with the bond stiffness

S_0 = \left(\frac{dF}{dr}\right)_{r_0} = \left(\frac{d^2U}{dr^2}\right)_{r_0}

Dividing force by the area per atom (\sigma = F/r_0^2) and stretch by the spacing (\varepsilon = (r - r_0)/r_0):

E \approx \frac{S_0}{r_0}

A steep F-r curve at r_0, that is a narrow, sharply curved energy well, gives a high Young's modulus.

Theoretical strength: the peak. Beyond r_0, F rises to a maximum F_{max} at r_m, the inflection point of U, then falls: a load above F_{max} pulls the atoms apart, so \sigma_{th} \approx F_{max}/r_0^2. Treating the curve beyond r_0 as a sine, \sigma = \sigma_{th}\sin(2\pi x/\lambda), and matching its initial slope to E/a_0:

\sigma_{th} = \frac{E\lambda}{2\pi a_0} \approx \frac{E}{2\pi} \approx \frac{E}{10} \quad (\lambda \approx a_0)

The same curve fixes both: a deep, steep curve gives a high slope and a high peak.

Ceramics. Strong ionic and covalent bonds give such curves: E \approx 380\ \mathrm{GPa} and \sigma_{th} \approx 38\ \mathrm{GPa} for \mathrm{Al_2O_3}. Real strengths are only E/100 to E/1000 because flaws concentrate stress (slide 7).
pts: Draws U(r) and F = dU/dr, with F = 0 at r_0 (energy minimum), attraction and repulsion
Stiffness from the slope at r_0: S_0 = (dF/dr)_{r_0} = (d^2U/dr^2)_{r_0} and E \approx S_0/r_0; steeper slope, higher E
Theoretical strength from the peak force F_{max} at the inflection of U: \sigma_{th} \approx F_{max}/r_0^2
Sine approximation gives \sigma_{th} \approx E\lambda/(2\pi a_0) \approx E/10, linking strength to stiffness through the curve shape
Compares a strong (ceramic: deep, steep) and a weak bond curve, with a value such as E \approx 380\ \mathrm{GPa} for alumina
Notes that measured strength is far below \sigma_{th} because of flaws
4c.src: Mechanical properties, slides 1, 7; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, pp 70-71, 341-342
4c.watch:
• Stiffness comes from the slope (curvature of U) at r_0, not from the well depth; the depth is the bond energy and tracks the melting point.
  • Carter's sign convention takes attraction as positive; electrostatics often uses the opposite. State yours on the sketch.
  • Including the surface energy, 2\gamma = area under the stress curve, gives the Orowan form \sigma_{th} = \sqrt{E\gamma/a_0}.

5b(i).html:
\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} on an \mathrm{Al^{3+}} site is \mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} (effective charge -1). Two Mg fill two Al sites, which need three O sites, but 2 MgO brings only two oxygens, so one O site stays empty:

2\mathrm{MgO} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Al_2O_3}\ } 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}

Mass: 2 Mg, 2 O. Sites: 2 Al to 3 O. Charge: -2 + 2 = 0, so [\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}}] = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}].

The interstitial alternative also balances:

3\mathrm{MgO} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{Al_2O_3}\ } 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + \mathrm{Mg_i^{\bullet\bullet}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}
pts: Writes Mg on an Al site as \mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}}
Balanced reaction 2\mathrm{MgO} \to 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}
Checks mass, the 2:3 site ratio and charge
Gives the interstitial (or hole) alternative or the electroneutrality condition
5b(i).src: Defects in ceramics: point defects and non-stoichiometry, slides 6, 13; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, p 206
5b(i).watch: • Keep the 2:3 site ratio of \mathrm{Al_2O_3}; 2\mathrm{MgO} \to 2\mathrm{Mg_{Al}^{\prime}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} creates an oxygen from nothing.

5b(ii).html:
In rock-salt BaO the only cation site is the Ba site, so \mathrm{Bi^{3+}} and \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} both become donors, \mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}} and \mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}}. The three oxygens of \mathrm{BiFeO_3} need three Ba sites; the third is left vacant:

\mathrm{BiFeO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{BaO}\ } \mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{V_{Ba}^{\prime\prime}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}

Mass: 1 Bi, 1 Fe, 3 O. Sites: 3 Ba to 3 O. Charge: +1 + 1 - 2 = 0.

At low p_{\mathrm{O_2}} electrons compensate instead:

\mathrm{BiFeO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{BaO}\ } \mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}} + 2\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2e^{\prime}
pts: Places both trivalent ions on Ba sites, \mathrm{Bi_{Ba}^{\bullet}} and \mathrm{Fe_{Ba}^{\bullet}}
Balanced reaction with \mathrm{V_{Ba}^{\prime\prime}} and 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}}
Checks mass, the 1:1 site ratio and charge
Gives the electronic alternative
5b(ii).src: Defects in ceramics: point defects and non-stoichiometry, slides 6, 13; Carter and Norton, Ceramic Materials, p 206
5b(ii).watch: • BaO is rock salt; do not put Fe on a "B site" as in a perovskite.

5c.html:
A compound becomes metal-deficient (oxygen-excess) when it takes up oxygen from the gas. The charge is balanced by oxidising some cations to a higher valence; these are the holes. Only cations with two stable valences can do this (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu, U; not Mg).

Reaction 1: cation vacancies (cations leave sites).

\tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}, \quad\text{or}\quad 2\mathrm{M_M^{\times}} + \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{M_M^{\bullet}} + \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}

The new O site needs a new M site, which stays empty. With p = 2[\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}], [\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}] = (K_1/4)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/6}.

Example: wustite \mathrm{Fe_{1-x}O} (also \mathrm{Ni_{1-x}O}, \mathrm{Co_{1-x}O}). Rock salt has a close-packed oxygen lattice with no room for extra oxygen, so cation vacancies form instead. \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} oxidises easily to \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}, so wustite never reaches FeO and is about \mathrm{Fe_{0.95}O}.

Reaction 2: oxygen interstitials.

\tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}, \qquad [\mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}}] = (K_2/4)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/6}

No cation site is needed; the extra oxide ion goes into an empty interstice.

Example: \mathrm{UO_{2+x}}. In fluorite, half of the oxygen cubes have an empty centre, a large site that can take an extra \mathrm{O^{2-}}, and \mathrm{U^{4+}} oxidises to \mathrm{U^{5+}} or \mathrm{U^{6+}}.

Both compounds are p-type, and their deviation from stoichiometry and conductivity rise with p_{\mathrm{O_2}}.
pts: Reaction 1 balanced: \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet} (holes may be written as \mathrm{M_M^{\bullet}})
Example for reaction 1, \mathrm{Fe_{1-x}O}, NiO or CoO, with the reason: close-packed rock-salt anions and a cation that oxidises from 2+ to 3+
Reaction 2 balanced: \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}
Example for reaction 2, \mathrm{UO_{2+x}}, with the reason: empty cube-centre interstices of fluorite and U with higher valences
Mass action: defect concentration proportional to p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/6}; p-type conduction rising with p_{\mathrm{O_2}}
States the general condition: the cation must have a higher stable valence (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu, U, not Mg)
5c.sketch:
• Panel (a): a missing cation labelled \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} and two neighbouring cations labelled \mathrm{M_M^{\bullet}} (\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}).
  • Panel (b): an extra anion in an interstice labelled \mathrm{O_i^{\prime\prime}} and two oxidised cations.

5c.watch:
• "Metal-deficient" and "oxygen-excess" describe the same composition shift; both reactions above qualify.
  • A third route is loss of metal to the vapour, \mathrm{M_M^{\times}} \to \mathrm{M(g)} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}, which gives the same defects as reaction 1.
  • Dissolving the higher oxide gives the same defects: \mathrm{Fe_2O_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{FeO}} 2\mathrm{Fe_{Fe}^{\bullet}} + 3\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_{Fe}^{\prime\prime}}.

6a.html:
In a non-stoichiometric oxide the oxygen content follows the gas. Every oxygen lost or gained creates ionic defects plus electrons or holes, so the carrier concentration, and with it \sigma = ne\mu_n + pe\mu_h, varies as a power of p_{\mathrm{O_2}}. The mobilities hardly depend on p_{\mathrm{O_2}}, so \sigma tracks the carrier concentration set by the mass-action law.

n-type, oxygen-deficient oxides (\mathrm{TiO_{2-x}}, \mathrm{ZrO_{2-x}}, \mathrm{CeO_{2-x}}):

\mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \rightleftharpoons \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime}, \qquad K_v = [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}]\,n^2\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{1/2}

Electroneutrality n = 2[\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}] gives n = (2K_v)^{1/3}p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6}. The electrons sit on \mathrm{Ti^{3+}} and \sigma falls as p_{\mathrm{O_2}} rises. Zn-excess ZnO (\mathrm{Zn_i^{\bullet}} + e^{\prime}) gives \sigma \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/4}.

p-type, metal-deficient oxides (\mathrm{Fe_{1-x}O}, \mathrm{Ni_{1-x}O}, \mathrm{Co_{1-x}O}):

\tfrac12\mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet}

With p = 2[\mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}}], p \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6}. Holes hop between \mathrm{M^{2+}} and \mathrm{M^{3+}}, and \sigma rises with p_{\mathrm{O_2}}.

Both regimes in one oxide. Undoped \mathrm{SrTiO_3} and \mathrm{BaTiO_3} are n-type at low p_{\mathrm{O_2}} (-1/6, then -1/4) and p-type at high p_{\mathrm{O_2}} (+1/4), with a minimum at n = p. In CaO-doped \mathrm{ZrO_2} the dopant fixes [\mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}}], so a flat ionic region separates the two branches: the electrolytic window used in oxygen sensors and fuel cells.

Use. With \sigma = \sigma_0\exp(-E_a/kT)\,p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{\pm 1/m}, a \mathrm{TiO_2} or \mathrm{BaTiO_3} element works as a resistive oxygen sensor.
pts: States that oxygen exchange with the gas creates ionic defects plus electrons or holes, so p_{\mathrm{O_2}} controls \sigma
Reduction reaction \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} \to \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} + \mathrm{V_O^{\bullet\bullet}} + 2e^{\prime} with its mass-action constant
Derives n \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{-1/6} with an n-type example (\mathrm{TiO_{2-x}}, \mathrm{CeO_{2-x}}, or ZnO with -1/4)
Oxidation reaction \tfrac12\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{O_O^{\times}} + \mathrm{V_M^{\prime\prime}} + 2h^{\bullet} with its mass-action constant
Derives p \propto p_{\mathrm{O_2}}^{+1/6} with a p-type example (\mathrm{Fe_{1-x}O}, NiO, CoO)
Describes an oxide with both regimes and a minimum (\mathrm{SrTiO_3}, \mathrm{BaTiO_3}) or the ionic plateau of CaO-doped \mathrm{ZrO_2}
Sketches \log\sigma against \log p_{\mathrm{O_2}} with correctly signed slopes

  • n-type line of slope -1/6 (\mathrm{TiO_{2-x}}) or -1/4 (ZnO); p-type line of slope +1/6 (NiO, \mathrm{Fe_{1-x}O}).
  • A V-shaped curve with its minimum at n = p (\mathrm{SrTiO_3}).

7a.html:
Ionic moments from the atomic numbers. \mathrm{Cd^{2+}} (Z = 48): [\mathrm{Kr}]4d^{10}, 0\,\mu_B. \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} (Z = 28): [\mathrm{Ar}]3d^8, 2 unpaired, 2\,\mu_B. \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (Z = 26): [\mathrm{Ar}]3d^5, 5 unpaired, 5\,\mu_B.

Cation distribution. \mathrm{NiFe_2O_4} is an inverse spinel. \mathrm{Cd^{2+}}, like \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}, has a strong tetrahedral (A) preference, so every Cd sends one \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} from A to B:

(\mathrm{Cd}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x})_A[\mathrm{Ni}_{1-x}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+x}]_B\mathrm{O_4}

Theoretical (Neel) moment. A-O-B superexchange, the strongest coupling, is antiferromagnetic, so the two sublattices subtract:

\begin{aligned} M_A &= 5(1-x), \qquad M_B = 2(1-x) + 5(1+x) = 7 + 3x \\ n_B &= M_B - M_A = 2 + 8x\ \ \mu_B\ \text{per formula unit} \end{aligned}
x00.20.40.60.81.0
n_B (\mu_B)2.03.65.26.88.410.0

The moment rises by 1.6\,\mu_B for every 0.2 of Cd: the non-magnetic ion empties the minority A sublattice and adds \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} to the majority B sublattice.

Why the experimental values fall near x of 0.5 (Yafet-Kittel model).

  1. In a spinel J_{AB} (A-O-B about 125^\circ) is strong and J_{BB} (90^\circ) is weak; both are antiferromagnetic. While J_{AB} dominates, all B moments are held parallel (Neel state).
  2. Cd removes magnetic A neighbours of each B ion, so the A-B molecular field on B falls roughly as (1-x); the B-B field stays.
  3. Near x \approx 0.4 to 0.5 the B-B antiferromagnetic interaction competes. The B sublattice splits into B_1 and B_2, each canted by \alpha_{YK} from the axis antiparallel to A, a triangular arrangement:
n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A
  1. Energy minimisation gives \cos\alpha_{YK} = \lambda_{AB}M_A/(\lambda_{BB}M_B), so the canted moment is n_B = M_A(\lambda_{AB}/\lambda_{BB} - 1) and falls with M_A = 5(1-x).
  2. At x = 1, \alpha_{YK} = 90^\circ and n_B \to 0: \mathrm{CdFe_2O_4} is not ferrimagnetic.

The falling Curie temperature with dilution lowers room-temperature values further.
pts: Moments from the configurations: \mathrm{Cd^{2+}} 4d^{10} 0, \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} 3d^8 2\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} 3d^5 5\,\mu_B

M_A = 5(1-x), M_B = 7 + 3x, n_B = 2 + 8x
Values 2.0, 3.6, 5.2, 6.8, 8.4, 10.0 \mu_B for x = 0 to 1
Dilution weakens the A-B field on B until the weak B-B antiferromagnetic coupling competes, near x \approx 0.5
Yafet-Kittel triangular arrangement: B split into B_1, B_2 canted by \pm\alpha_{YK}, sketched
n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A, with \alpha_{YK} \to 90^\circ and n_B \to 0 as x \to 1

7b.html:
Given: r_{\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}} = 0.074\ \mathrm{nm}, r_{\mathrm{Co^{2+}}} = 0.0745\ \mathrm{nm}, r_{\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}} = 0.0645\ \mathrm{nm}, R_O = 0.142\ \mathrm{nm}; (i) x = 0.1; (ii) x = 0.8 with \alpha_{YK} = 80^\circ.

Find: the saturation moment n_B (\mu_B per formula unit) and the lattice parameter a.

Solution

Step 1, distribution and ionic moments. \mathrm{CoFe_2O_4} is inverse and \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} goes to A:

(\mathrm{Zn}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x})_A[\mathrm{Co}_{1-x}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+x}]_B\mathrm{O_4}

Spin-only moments from the unpaired 3d electrons: \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (3d^5) 5\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Co^{2+}} (3d^7) 3\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} (3d^{10}) 0.

Step 2, sublattice moments. The A-O-B superexchange (bond angle about 125^\circ) is the strongest coupling in a spinel and is antiferromagnetic, so all A moments are parallel to each other and antiparallel to all B moments:

M_A = 5(1-x), \qquad M_B = 3(1-x) + 5(1+x)

Collinear (Neel) model: n_B = M_B - M_A. When much of the A site is non-magnetic Zn, each B ion has few magnetic A neighbours, the weak B-B antiferromagnetic exchange competes, and the B sublattice splits into two halves canted by \alpha_{YK} from the B axis (Yafet-Kittel). Only the component along the axis survives:

n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A

Step 3, lattice parameter (ideal spinel, one A and two B sites):

a = \frac{8}{3\sqrt{3}}\left[(r_A + R_O) + \sqrt{3}\,(r_B + R_O)\right], \quad r_A = x r_{\mathrm{Zn}} + (1-x) r_{\mathrm{Fe}}, \quad r_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[(1-x) r_{\mathrm{Co}} + (1+x) r_{\mathrm{Fe}}\right]

(i) x = 0.1

Little Zn, so the A-B coupling dominates and the arrangement is collinear:

\begin{aligned} M_A &= 5(0.9) = 4.5\,\mu_B, \qquad M_B = 3(0.9) + 5(1.1) = 8.2\,\mu_B \\ n_B &= 8.2 - 4.5 = 3.7\,\mu_B \\ r_A &= 0.1(0.074) + 0.9(0.0645) = 0.06545\ \mathrm{nm}, \qquad r_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[0.9(0.0745) + 1.1(0.0645)\right] = 0.0690\ \mathrm{nm} \\ a &= 1.5396\left[0.20745 + 1.7321(0.2110)\right] = 0.8821\ \mathrm{nm} \end{aligned}

(ii) x = 0.8, alpha_YK = 80 degrees

\begin{aligned} M_A &= 5(0.2) = 1.0\,\mu_B, \qquad M_B = 3(0.2) + 5(1.8) = 9.6\,\mu_B \\ n_B &= 9.6\cos 80^\circ - 1.0 = 9.6(0.1736) - 1.0 = 0.67\,\mu_B \quad (\text{Neel: } 8.6\,\mu_B) \\ r_A &= 0.8(0.074) + 0.2(0.0645) = 0.0721\ \mathrm{nm}, \qquad r_B = \tfrac{1}{2}\left[0.2(0.0745) + 1.8(0.0645)\right] = 0.0655\ \mathrm{nm} \\ a &= 1.5396\left[0.2141 + 1.7321(0.2075)\right] = 0.8830\ \mathrm{nm} \end{aligned}

Answer: (i) n_B = 3.7\,\mu_B per formula unit, a = 0.882 nm; (ii) n_B = 0.67\,\mu_B per formula unit, a = 0.883 nm. With 8 formula units per cell, M_s = 8n_B\mu_B/a^3 is about 400 kA/m and 72 kA/m. The lattice parameter barely changes because r_{\mathrm{Zn}} \approx r_{\mathrm{Co}}. At x = 0.8 the A sublattice is so diluted that the B-B exchange cants the B moments, and the moment falls far below the Neel value.
pts: Cation distribution with Zn on A and inverse Co ferrite: (\mathrm{Zn}_x\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x})_A[\mathrm{Co}_{1-x}\mathrm{Fe}_{1+x}]_B\mathrm{O_4}
Ionic moments \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} 5\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Co^{2+}} 3\,\mu_B, \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} 0, from unpaired 3d electrons
(i) M_A = 4.5, M_B = 8.2, antiparallel, so n_B = 3.7\,\mu_B per formula unit
Lattice-parameter relation a = \frac{8}{3\sqrt{3}}[(r_A + R_O) + \sqrt{3}(r_B + R_O)] with site-averaged radii
(i) r_A = 0.06545 nm, r_B = 0.0690 nm, a = 0.882 nm
(ii) Yafet-Kittel net moment n_B = M_B\cos\alpha_{YK} - M_A, with only the B sublattice canted
(ii) M_A = 1.0, M_B = 9.6, n_B = 9.6\cos 80^\circ - 1.0 = 0.67\,\mu_B (against 8.6 for Neel)
(ii) r_A = 0.0721 nm, r_B = 0.0655 nm, a = 0.883 nm
States the result with units (\mu_B per formula unit, nm) and explains the almost constant a (r_{\mathrm{Zn}} \approx r_{\mathrm{Co}}) and the collapse of n_B by canting

7b.watch:
• The printed radii are six-coordinate values with R_O = 0.142 nm, so a comes out near 0.88 nm, about 5% above measured \mathrm{CoFe_2O_4} (0.839 nm). Use the printed values; the trend is the point.
  • Apply \cos\alpha_{YK} to M_B only. The A moments stay collinear; it is the B sublattice that splits into two canted halves.
  • Real \mathrm{CoFe_2O_4} is only partly inverse, and \mathrm{Co^{2+}} keeps some orbital moment (measured about 3.7\,\mu_B per formula unit rather than 3, 435-mag3 slide 40). The question expects the spin-only, fully inverse model.
  • A canting angle is not printed for (i); at x = 0.1 the arrangement is collinear (\alpha_{YK} = 0).
  • The paper labels the iron radius r_{\mathrm{Fe}}^{2+}, but 0.0645 nm is the radius of high-spin \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} (\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} is about 0.078 nm), and all the iron in this ferrite is \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}. Read it as \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}.

8a.html:
The dielectric constant is \varepsilon_r = 1 + \chi_e + \chi_i + \chi_d + \chi_s, so it changes whenever one of the four polarisation mechanisms starts or stops working.

Frequency. Each mechanism contributes only while its charges can follow the field reversals, so \varepsilon_r' falls in steps as frequency rises. Space charge drops out above about 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz and dipolar orientation relaxes at about 10^{7} to 10^{9} Hz. Ionic polarisation is lost at about 10^{13} Hz and electronic at about 10^{15} Hz (resonances). At optical frequencies \varepsilon_r = n^2 (water: 80 falls to 1.77), and the loss \varepsilon'' peaks at every step.

Temperature.

  • Electronic and ionic: almost independent of T; thermal expansion changes them only slightly.
  • Dipolar: thermal agitation opposes alignment, \alpha_d = \mu^2/3kT, so \varepsilon_r falls as T rises. Dipoles frozen in a solid make \varepsilon_r jump when they become free.
  • Space charge: ion mobility is thermally activated, so the low-frequency \varepsilon_r and loss rise steeply at high T.
  • Ferroelectrics: \varepsilon_r peaks at the Curie point (\mathrm{BaTiO_3}, 120 °C, about 10^{4}) and falls above it by the Curie-Weiss law, \varepsilon_r = C/(T - T_0).
pts: States that \varepsilon_r is the sum of the mechanism contributions and that each drops out above its limiting frequency, so \varepsilon_r' falls stepwise with frequency
Gives the order and ranges: space charge about 10^{2} to 10^{3} Hz, dipolar about 10^{9} Hz, ionic about 10^{13} Hz, electronic about 10^{15} Hz, with \varepsilon_r = n^2 at optical frequencies
Notes the loss peak at each step
Electronic and ionic polarisation are nearly independent of temperature
Dipolar: \alpha_d = \mu^2/3kT, so \varepsilon_r falls as temperature rises
Space charge: thermally activated, raising the low-frequency \varepsilon_r and loss at high temperature
Ferroelectric: peak at the Curie point (\mathrm{BaTiO_3} 120 °C) with Curie-Weiss behaviour above it
Sketches \varepsilon_r against log frequency or against temperature
8a.sketch:
• \varepsilon_r' against log f: falling staircase with resonance swings near 10^{13} and 10^{15} Hz.
  • \varepsilon_r against T for \mathrm{BaTiO_3}: sharp peak at 120 °C, Curie-Weiss fall above it.

• "tem" in the printed question is a typing slip for temperature.

8b.html:
Given: Q = 4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C}, V = 10{,}000\ \mathrm{V}, d = 0.2\ \mathrm{mm} = 2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}; \kappa' = 1 (vacuum), 2.26 (polyethylene), 78.3 (water), 3000 (\mathrm{BaTiO_3}); \varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}.

Find: the plate area for dielectrics (a) to (d).

Solution. The charge and voltage fix the capacitance; the parallel-plate formula then gives the area:

\begin{aligned} C &= \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{4\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{C}}{10^{4}\ \mathrm{V}} = 4\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{F} \\ C &= \frac{\kappa'\varepsilon_0A}{d} \quad\Rightarrow\quad A = \frac{Cd}{\kappa'\varepsilon_0} = \frac{(4\times10^{-9})(2\times10^{-4})}{\kappa'(8.854\times10^{-12})}\ \mathrm{m^2} = \frac{9.04\times10^{-2}}{\kappa'}\ \mathrm{m^2} \end{aligned}
Dielectric\kappa'A (\mathrm{m^2})A (\mathrm{cm^2})
(a) vacuum19.04\times10^{-2}904
(b) polyethylene2.264.00\times10^{-2}400
(c) water78.31.15\times10^{-3}11.5
(d) \mathrm{BaTiO_3}30003.01\times10^{-5}0.301

Answer: (a) 0.090\ \mathrm{m^2}, (b) 0.040\ \mathrm{m^2}, (c) 1.15\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}, (d) 3.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2}.

Comment. Because A \propto 1/\kappa', the same charge at the same voltage needs a plate about 30 cm square in vacuum but only a disc about 6 mm across with \mathrm{BaTiO_3}, which is why ferroelectric ceramics are the capacitor dielectric of choice. The field in every case is V/d = 5\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}. That exceeds the dielectric strengths on slide 8 (polyethylene 20, \mathrm{BaTiO_3} 12\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}), so a working design needs a thicker dielectric or a multilayer stack.

(a) Vacuum: A \approx 0.090\ \mathrm{m^2}

• Keep SI units throughout: d in metres, so A comes out in \mathrm{m^2}; quote \mathrm{cm^2} only as a second unit.
